proposals.before: Wang Shan, whose style was Zaosru, came from Taicang in Jiangnan. He was the grandson of the Ming Grand Secretary Xijue.
proposals.after: Wang Shan, whose style was Zaoru, came from Taicang in Jiangnan. He was the grandson of the Ming Grand Secretary Xijue.
proposals.reason: Chinese 藻儒 is Zaoru; idiomatic Zaosru is a clear misspelling.

proposals.before: Wang Shan, style Zaosru, was a native of Taicang in Jiangnan; he was the grandson of Xijue, Grand Secretary of the Ming.
proposals.after: Wang Shan, style Zaoru, was a native of Taicang in Jiangnan; he was the grandson of Xijue, Grand Secretary of the Ming.
proposals.reason: Chinese 藻儒 is Zaoru; literal Zaosru is a clear misspelling.

proposals.before: In 1691 he was specially promoted to Grand Secretary of the Grand Secretariat.
proposals.after: In 1691 he was specially promoted to Academician of the Grand Secretariat.
proposals.reason: 內閣學士 is Academician of the Grand Secretariat, not Grand Secretary (大學士).

proposals.before: In the thirtieth year he was promoted by special selection to Grand Secretary of the Grand Secretariat.
proposals.after: In the thirtieth year he was promoted by special selection to Academician of the Grand Secretariat.
proposals.reason: 內閣學士 is Academician of the Grand Secretariat, not Grand Secretary (大學士).

decisions.reason: s0004 gives 字藻儒; 藻儒 is Zaoru, so idiomatic Zaosru is a misspelling. The proposed Zaoru restores the correct courtesy name without other changes.
The same 藻儒 requires Zaoru in the literal field; Zaosru is a misspelling, and the proposed replacement is accurate.
s0011 has 超擢內閣學士; 內閣學士 is Academician of the Grand Secretariat, distinct from 大學士 Grand Secretary. The prior idiomatic conflates the ranks; the proposed title is correct.
Literal likewise renders 內閣學士 as Grand Secretary; Academician of the Grand Secretariat matches the Chinese office and leaves the rest of the sentence intact.
